title: What is matter?

authored.application: Recognizing matter helps us choose ways to store, measure, separate and safely use materials.
authored.explanation: Matter is made of tiny particles. Air, water, a book and your body are matter; light and sound are forms of energy and are not matter.
authored.relationship: matter -> has mass + occupies space
authored.example: Example: an inflated football has more mass than the same football when empty because the added air is matter and occupies space.

authored.explanation: The familiar states are solid, liquid and gas. Plasma occurs at very high energy, while a Bose-Einstein condensate forms near absolute zero.

authored.explanation: Orbitals are not fixed paths. The s subshell has one orbital, p has three, d has five and f has seven; their shapes and orientations affect bonding.

authored.explanation: The usual filling order follows increasing n + l; when two subshells have equal n + l, the one with lower n fills first. Some transition elements have exceptions.
authored.relationship: lower orbital energy fills first; use the n + l rule

authored.explanation: Spreading electrons across degenerate orbitals reduces repulsion and gives a lower-energy arrangement.

authored.explanation: Therefore one orbital holds at most two electrons, and those two must have opposite spins.
authored.relationship: one orbital -> maximum 2 electrons with opposite spins

title: Calorimetry

authored.application: Lattice energy helps explain melting point, solubility, stability and hardness of ionic solids.
authored.explanation: Its magnitude increases with larger ionic charges and smaller ion separation. Sign conventions differ, so specify whether formation or separation is meant.

title: Born-Haber cycle

authored.summary: A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess Law to ionic-solid formation.

authored.application: Born-Haber cycles compare ionic stability, lattice energy and plausibility of oxidation states.
authored.explanation: It combines atomization, ionization, electron affinity, bond dissociation and lattice steps so an unmeasurable lattice enthalpy can be inferred.
authored.relationship: deltaHformation = sum of atom and ion steps + lattice enthalpy
authored.example: Example: a NaCl cycle links sodium sublimation, chlorine bond dissociation, sodium ionization, chlorine electron gain and NaCl lattice formation.

title: Ideal and non-ideal solutions

authored.summary: Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law throughout the composition range; non-ideal solutions show positive or negative deviations because unlike-molecule attractions differ from like-molecule attractions.
authored.mistake: Do not label a solution ideal merely because both components are liquids; compare the measured vapour pressure and mixing effects with Raoult's-law predictions.
authored.application: Vapour-pressure diagrams and azeotropes determine whether industrial liquid mixtures can be separated by ordinary fractional distillation.
authored.explanation: For an ideal binary solution, each partial vapour pressure is pi = xi pi° and the total is their sum. DeltaHmix and DeltaVmix are zero. Weaker A-B attractions produce positive deviation, higher vapour pressure and often a minimum-boiling azeotrope; stronger A-B attractions produce negative deviation and may form a maximum-boiling azeotrope.
authored.relationship: pi = xi pi°; ptotal = sum(pi); ideal: DeltaHmix = 0 and DeltaVmix = 0
authored.example: Example: at a fixed temperature, xA = 0.40, pA° = 100 kPa, xB = 0.60 and pB° = 50 kPa. ptotal = 0.40(100) + 0.60(50) = 70 kPa. A measured value above 70 kPa indicates positive deviation.

title: Abnormal molar mass and van't Hoff factor

authored.summary: Solute association or dissociation changes the number of dissolved particles, producing an apparent molar mass different from the true value.
authored.mistake: Do not automatically use the integer number of ions as i; incomplete dissociation and ion pairing make experimental i non-integral.
authored.application: Van't Hoff corrections improve molar-mass determination and electrolyte formulation in pharmaceuticals, antifreeze and physiological solutions.
authored.explanation: The van't Hoff factor i is the observed colligative property divided by the value expected for a non-electrolyte. Dissociation normally gives i greater than one; association gives i less than one. For dissociation into nu particles, i = 1 + alpha(nu - 1); for n-mer association, i = 1 - alpha(1 - 1/n).
authored.relationship: i = observed colligative property / calculated value; DeltaTf = i Kf m
authored.example: Example: 0.10 mol CaCl2 in 1.0 kg water gives depression in freezing point 0.465 K when Kf = 1.86 K kg mol-1. i = 0.465/(1.86 x 0.10) = 2.50; alpha = (2.50 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 0.75.

title: Colligative-property numericals

authored.summary: Relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure depend on the number of solute particles rather than their chemical identity.
authored.mistake: Do not use grams of solvent where kilograms are required, and do not substitute solution volume into a molality calculation.

Include i for association or dissociation. Osmotic pressure is preferred for macromolecules because it can be measured at room temperature using very dilute solutions.

authored.example: Example: 1.80 g glucose is dissolved in 100 g water. Moles = 1.80/180 = 0.0100 and m = 0.0100/0.100 = 0.100 mol kg-1. With Kf(water) = 1.86 K kg mol-1, DeltaTf = 0.186 K and the freezing point is -0.186 °C.

title: Dynamic equilibrium

authored.summary: Dynamic equilibrium occurs when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a closed system.

authored.application: Dynamic equilibrium controls industrial synthesis, gas binding, solubility and acid-base systems.
authored.explanation: Macroscopic concentrations remain constant even though both reactions continue microscopically. Equilibrium can be reached from either direction.
authored.relationship: rateforward = ratereverse
authored.example: Example: in N2O4(g) <-> 2NO2(g), molecules continue interconverting while the colour and concentrations remain constant at equilibrium.

authored.application: Equilibrium constants predict yield, dissociation, solubility and acid-base composition.
authored.explanation: Each term is raised to its stoichiometric coefficient; pure solids and liquids are omitted. K changes with temperature but not with initial composition.

authored.application: The principle guides ammonia manufacture, gas reactions, buffers and product recovery.
authored.explanation: The system shifts in the direction that partly opposes a concentration, pressure or temperature change. A catalyst speeds approach but does not shift equilibrium.
authored.relationship: disturbance -> shift that reduces its effect

authored.application: Molecularity connects proposed mechanisms with elementary-step rate laws.

title: Integrated rate equations

authored.summary: Integrated rate laws connect reactant concentration with time and allow reaction order and rate constants to be extracted from experimental data.

authored.explanation: For a zero-order reaction, [A]t = [A]0 - kt and [A] versus t is linear. For first order, ln[A]t = ln[A]0 - kt and ln[A] versus t is linear. The slope is -k, with units mol L-1 s-1 for zero order and s-1 for first order.
authored.relationship: zero: [A]t=[A]0-kt; first: k=(2.303/t)log([A]0/[A]t)

title: Half-life of reactions

authored.summary: Half-life is the time required for a reactant concentration to fall to half its current value, and its concentration dependence reveals reaction order.
authored.mistake: Do not apply the radioactive or first-order half-life formula to a zero-order reaction without first establishing the reaction order.
authored.application: Half-life calculations guide pharmaceutical expiry, radiotracer use, environmental persistence and reaction scheduling.
authored.explanation: For zero order, t1/2 = [A]0/(2k), so half-life decreases as the initial concentration decreases. For first order, t1/2 = ln2/k and is independent of initial concentration. Successive first-order halvings therefore take equal times.
authored.example: Example: if a first-order process has k = 2.31 x 10^-3 s-1, t1/2 = 0.693/k = 300 s. After three half-lives, the fraction remaining is (1/2)^3 = 1/8.

authored.example: Example: two molecules may collide often but react slowly when Ea is high or their reactive sites do not meet. A catalyst supplies another pathway with lower Ea, increasing effective collisions without changing DeltaG° or K.

authored.application: Arrhenius analysis predicts shelf life, process rates and temperature sensitivity.
authored.explanation: A is the pre-exponential factor and exp(-Ea/RT) represents the fraction of suitably energetic events. A plot of ln k against 1/T has slope -Ea/R.
authored.relationship: k = A exp(-Ea/RT)

title: Crystallisation of dissolved solids

authored.summary: Crystallisation purifies a dissolved solid by forming ordered crystals from a hot concentrated solution as it cools.
authored.mistake: Do not evaporate all the solvent to dryness: rapid complete evaporation can trap impurities and gives poorer crystals.
authored.application: Crystallisation purifies salt, sugar, pharmaceuticals and laboratory reagents while offering better purity than evaporation alone.
authored.explanation: Choose a solvent in which the solute is much more soluble when hot than cold. Dissolve the impure solid in minimum hot solvent, hot-filter insoluble impurities, concentrate if needed, cool without disturbance, filter the crystals, wash with a little cold solvent and dry. Soluble impurities largely remain in the mother liquor.
authored.relationship: hot saturated solution -> cooling -> crystals + mother liquor
authored.example: Example: Copper sulfate containing insoluble dirt is dissolved in hot water and filtered. Blue crystals form on slow cooling while much of the soluble impurity stays in solution.

title: Simple distillation of liquid mixtures

authored.summary: Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from a nonvolatile solute or from another liquid with a sufficiently different boiling point.
authored.mistake: Do not seal a distillation apparatus or heat a flask to complete dryness, and do not confuse distillation with simple evaporation because the solvent is recovered.
authored.application: Distillation supports water purification, solvent recovery and preparation of distilled laboratory water.
authored.explanation: Heat the mixture safely, allow the more volatile component to vaporise, cool the vapour in a condenser and collect the distillate. A thermometer measures vapour temperature near the condenser entrance. Anti-bumping measures and an open receiving path prevent sudden boiling and pressure buildup.
authored.relationship: liquid mixture --heating--> vapour --condensation--> distillate
authored.example: Example: Distilling salt water produces liquid water as distillate while dissolved salt remains in the flask; filtration could not remove that dissolved salt.

title: Paper chromatography

authored.summary: Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances because they travel differently with a solvent over paper.
authored.mistake: Do not draw the baseline in ink or immerse the sample spot in solvent; either action contaminates or washes away the starting sample.
authored.application: Chromatography separates inks, food colours, plant pigments and components used in forensic or quality-control comparisons.
authored.explanation: Place a small sample spot on a pencil baseline above the solvent. The solvent rises by capillary action; components repeatedly partition between the mobile solvent and stationary water/paper environment. Mark the solvent front immediately and compare spots using Rf under identical conditions.
authored.relationship: Rf = distance travelled by solute / distance travelled by solvent front; 0 <= Rf <= 1
authored.example: Example: If an ink dye travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm, Rf = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60.

title: Sublimation as a separation method

authored.summary: Sublimation separates a solid that changes directly to vapour from non-subliming solids.
authored.mistake: Do not call ordinary evaporation sublimation; sublimation begins with a solid and bypasses the liquid state under the stated conditions.
authored.application: Sublimation is used to purify volatile solids and illustrates particle motion during direct solid-gas changes.
authored.explanation: Heat the mixture gently under an inverted funnel or cold surface. The sublimable component forms vapour and deposits as solid on the cooler surface, while the nonvolatile component remains. Suitable examples include ammonium chloride, camphor or naphthalene mixed with sand or salt.

authored.example: Example: On gently heating ammonium chloride mixed with sodium chloride, ammonium chloride deposits on the cool funnel while sodium chloride remains in the dish.

title: Centrifugation of mixtures

authored.summary: Centrifugation speeds separation by spinning a mixture so denser suspended particles move outward and settle faster.
authored.mistake: Never run a centrifuge with unbalanced tubes, an unsecured lid or cracked containers; imbalance can damage the rotor and injure users.
authored.application: Centrifugation is used in dairies, clinical blood processing, wastewater treatment and laboratory sample preparation.
authored.explanation: Opposing tubes must have equal masses and be placed symmetrically. After spinning at the specified speed and time, the dense sediment is the pellet and the liquid above it is the supernatant. Centrifugation helps when particles are too small or slow to settle by gravity alone.
authored.relationship: greater density difference and rotation -> faster sedimentation
authored.example: Example: A milk separator uses spinning to divide components of different density; a laboratory centrifuge can separate fine chalk from water into pellet and supernatant.

title: Coagulation of colloids

authored.summary: Coagulation makes tiny colloidal particles combine into larger aggregates that can settle or be filtered.
authored.mistake: Do not describe coagulation as dissolving dirt or as filtration itself; it changes particle aggregation so later settling and filtration work better.
authored.application: Coagulation clarifies drinking water, treats wastewater and supports food and materials processing.
authored.explanation: Colloid particles often carry like charges that keep them dispersed. Adding a suitable electrolyte, heating, mixing oppositely charged sols or controlled stirring can reduce this stabilisation. In water treatment, coagulant produces flocs that capture suspended material before settling and filtration.
authored.relationship: destabilised colloid particles -> flocs -> settling or filtration
authored.example: Example: Alum added during water treatment forms flocs that trap fine suspended dirt; the larger flocs settle more readily than individual colloidal particles.

title: Concentration calculations

authored.summary: Concentration states how much solute is present in a specified amount of solution.
authored.mistake: Do not divide by solvent amount when the definition asks for solution amount, and do not mix grams with kilograms or millilitres with litres without conversion.
authored.application: Concentration calculations guide medicines, beverages, cleaning solutions, agriculture and laboratory preparation.
authored.explanation: Class 9 calculations use mass-by-mass percentage, mass-by-volume percentage and volume-by-volume percentage. Identify whether the denominator is mass or volume of the complete solution, use compatible units and include the percent sign. The mass of solution equals solute plus solvent mass.

authored.example: Example: A solution made from 10 g salt and 90 g water has total mass 100 g, so mass percentage = 10/100 x100 = 10%.

title: Solubility curves and graphs

authored.summary: A solubility curve shows the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in a fixed mass of solvent at different temperatures.
authored.mistake: Do not assume every solid becomes more soluble at the same rate with temperature; read the specific curve and its axis units.
authored.application: Solubility graphs help design crystallisation, compare substances and predict whether a solution is saturated.
authored.explanation: Read temperature on the horizontal axis and solubility—often grams solute per 100 g water—on the vertical axis. A point below the curve is unsaturated, on the curve saturated and above the curve represents excess solute or a supersaturated condition if temporarily maintained. The difference between hot and cold solubility predicts crystallisation yield.
authored.relationship: crystals expected = solute dissolved hot - solute remaining dissolved cold
authored.example: Example: If 80 g solute dissolves in 100 g water at 80 °C but only 30 g at 20 °C, ideal cooling can produce 50 g crystals.

title: Formation of ionic and covalent compounds

authored.summary: Ionic compounds form through electron transfer and electrostatic attraction, while covalent compounds form through sharing electron pairs.
authored.mistake: Do not describe an ionic compound as a molecule made of one ion pair; an ionic solid contains a repeating lattice of oppositely charged ions.

authored.explanation: Metals commonly lose valence electrons to form cations and non-metals gain them to form anions. Between non-metals, shared pairs allow atoms to approach stable outer-shell configurations. Charge balance determines ionic formulae; shared-pair count determines covalent structure.
authored.relationship: ionic: Na -> Na+ + e- and Cl + e- -> Cl-; covalent: H:H
authored.example: Example: Magnesium loses two electrons and two chlorine atoms each gain one, forming Mg2+ and 2Cl-, hence MgCl2. Two hydrogen atoms share one pair to form H2.

title: Properties of ionic versus covalent compounds

authored.summary: Ionic and covalent compounds show different bulk properties because their particles and bonding structures differ.
authored.mistake: Do not claim every covalent substance has a low melting point or is insoluble in water; structure, polarity and intermolecular forces create exceptions.
authored.application: Comparing compound properties guides material selection, electrolyte use and safe interpretation of laboratory tests.
authored.explanation: Ionic solids usually have high melting points, are brittle and conduct only when molten or dissolved because ions must move. Simple covalent substances often have lower melting/boiling points and usually do not conduct because they lack mobile charged particles. Giant covalent structures such as diamond are important exceptions.
authored.relationship: mobile ions -> electrical conduction; fixed lattice ions -> no solid-state conduction
authored.example: Example: Solid NaCl does not light a conductivity tester, but molten or aqueous NaCl can. Sugar solution generally does not conduct strongly because sugar remains as neutral molecules.

title: Endothermic and exothermic reactions

authored.summary: Exothermic reactions transfer heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings.
authored.mistake: A reaction that needs ignition is not necessarily endothermic; combustion needs activation energy but releases more energy overall.

authored.explanation: In an exothermic process the surroundings warm and products have lower enthalpy than reactants; in an endothermic process the surroundings cool and products have higher enthalpy. Activation energy is still required to begin either type.

title: Designing a fair chemistry investigation

authored.summary: A fair investigation changes one independent variable, measures a dependent variable and controls other factors that could affect the result.
authored.mistake: Do not change several variables at once or write a conclusion before inspecting the measurements and their variation.
authored.application: Experimental design supports trustworthy school practicals, product testing, environmental investigations and scientific decision-making.

Sample size and repeatability make the conclusion more reliable.
authored.relationship: question -> hypothesis -> variables -> method -> evidence -> conclusion

title: Representing chemistry data in tables and graphs

authored.summary: Well-designed tables and graphs reveal patterns while preserving units, uncertainty and the distinction between measured and calculated values.
authored.mistake: Do not omit units, force a graph through the origin without scientific reason or delete an anomalous result merely to improve the trend.
authored.application: Accurate data representation supports solubility analysis, reaction comparisons, calibration and clear scientific communication.
authored.explanation: Place the independent variable in the first table column and on the horizontal graph axis; place the dependent variable on the vertical axis.
